reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The noteworthy results are the improved on stream performance due to reduced coking. This is a very active area of research and there are lots of groups trying to develop materials for efficient direct deoxygenation of biofuel-related materials to improve the heating value of the materials. As an example, Fuel (334) 2023 "Enhanced deoxygenation performance and coke resistance of Ni-based catalysts for jatropha oil conversion by rare earth elements" is one such example. It is often difficult to compare one catalytic paper to another because there are so many variables, but while this paper represents a nice result, it is difficult to describe it as particularly novel or particularly significant. The experimental result is a bit underdeveloped in parts. The uploaded file provides more detail on what aspects need to be expanded. It also notes grammatical errors. As written there is not enough detail in the experimental section for the work to be reproduced, but this could be addressed in a revision. More detail is also needed on number of replicates and error propagation needs to be clearly articulated and error bars included on all catalytic data. The structure of the manuscript undercuts its potential impact. The whole idea of spending 12 pages discussing the first generation catalyst only to then switch to a second generation catalyst does not seem like an efficient or effective way to present this information. The aper would be more impactful if it begins with what works best and perhaps the discussion of the first generation catalyst can be mentioned briefly and mostly moved to SI.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: In this manuscript, the authors study TiO2-functionalized, bimetallic catalysts for hydrodeoxygenation of m-cresol, which is a much-studied reaction. This work essentially combines two ideas that have been in the literature for a while: adding Sn to Ni to reduce the tendency toward coke formation, and using TiO2 modifiers on the surface of the catalyst to improve interfacial activity. The authors discover some interesting synergistic effects. For example, whereas TiO2-supported Ni3Sn catalysts are active but not especially stable, producing inverse catalysts in which the TiO2 is located above the catalyst particles produces an active and stable catalyst. The authors largely do an excellent job of characterizing the prepared materials and analyzing the key reaction process with computational methods. Although some of the basic concepts that motivated the paper have been well-established, for me there is clearly sufficient novelty in the results to justify publication in Nature Comm. I recommend that the authors consider the following few points as they revise their manuscript. 1. Regarding Figure 1C, did the authors perform a control in which DRIFTS was done after adsorption of cresol on the support only? Sometimes it can be difficult to use DRIFTS to probe interfacial sites specifically, and some of these compounds may adsorb on support sites far from the interface. 2. The authors claim that the inverse strategy is beneficial because the TiOx on the surface has a lower acidity, allowing improved lifetime. However, I did not see where this proposal was tested experimentally. Can the authors elaborate on the evidence that supports their proposal? An alternative proposal is that TiO2 could block sites that ultimately lead to coking. I understand why the authors proposed that surface acidity is the driving factor, but the manuscript would be improved by describing the evidence for this proposal. 3. Since the TiO2 clusters appear from experimental data to bind to undercoordinated sites on the catalyst surface, did the DFT studies consider use of a stepped surface rather than a (111) surface for any exploratory calculations? Even if not, could the authors comment on whether the (111) surface would be expected to serve as a useful model? 4. Although the mechanistic proposal from the DFT calculations seems similar to that from Janik and coworkers (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcat.2019.07.012), the authors may want to comment more on the subsequent steps of the catalytic cycle, as in the prior work. It is not so surprising that a reduced Ti3O5 cluster will interact strongly with the O atom of m-cresol, especially on a Sn-doped surface where the interaction of the cluster with the surface is weaker. The key step on such a surface may be regeneration of the oxygen vacancy, which is only briefly discussed here in reference Figure S17. It wasn’t so clear to me: did the authors compute the activation barrier for oxygen vacancy creation? It appears that the energy required to create such a vacancy was similar for the Ni and Ni3Sn surfaces, which I find somewhat surprising given the other effects of Sn. In any case, I think the authors should talk more about the full cycle. Minor comments / typos: Line 138: “In contract” should be “In contrast” Line 192: “chemistry” should be “chemical” Line 205: the word “spectroscopy” should appear after “transform”, and the acronym should say “DRIFTS”. Line 448: “strength” should be “strong”
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: This work reports on the study of TiOx-modified Ni(Sn) catalysts for the hydrodeoxygenation of m-cresol through reactivity measurements, characterization, and theoretical calculations. The work follows a consistent narrative which introduces logically increasing complexity, first through the formation of NiSn alloy nanoparticles to improve HDO reactivity and stability over Ni nanoparticles, followed by the decoration of NiSn alloy nanoparticles with TiOx to facilitate reactivity. The authors conclude that TiOx and NiSn phases interact synergistically to enable enhanced HDO by reduced C-O activation barriers and inhibited deactivation mechanisms. However, there are some questions that remain after reading the manuscript as is that should be addressed prior to consideration for publication. Those questions are: 1. Through the manuscript, the authors are inconsistent in their assignment of deactivation behaviors. At times, they cite work which relates the formation of oxide overlayers (SMSI) to the deactivation of Ni sites by physical coverage and prevention of adsorption. Other times, they discuss the formation of coke at acidic TiOx sites. In the end, there does not seem to be a conclusion reached on which is relevant, or whether both contribute in this experimental system and sometimes the authors could be more quantitative. 2. For example, in the comparison of Ni/TiO2 and Ni/SiO2, the TiO2 supported material deactivates from 95 to 5% conversion whereas Ni/SiO2 deactivates from 95% to 50% conversion. Is this consistent with the 2x amount of C deposition for Ni/TiO2 compared to Ni/SiO2? 3. Staying on the note about deactivation – the authors focus on the acidity of TiO2 as a mediator for coke formation and thus deactivation. Upon formation of interaction between Sn and TiOx, the authors observe increased stability – this would lead one to consider that Sn has reduced the acidity of TiOx. How would this happen? What chemical effect would lead to this? 4. The estimation of TiOx coverage by CO DRIFTS is potentially not reliable, which the authors attempt to convey by calling the results “semi-quantitative”. Can the authors provide further detail about their DRIFTS quantification so that an assessment of the validity of their approach can be made? Is the quantification different if absorbance units are used instead of Kubelka-Munk? Is it possible to conduct a more quantitative analysis such as CO pulsed chemisorption? 5. Do the authors have insight into the experimental error for their temperature-dependent reaction measurements made to assess apparent activation barriers? What is the statistical significance of the difference in barriers between these two materials? 6. I have questions about the H/D exchange experiments and their analysis. The authors approach the data with the assumption that H2(D2) activation is rate-limiting in the case of all catalysts. Could it not also be that HD desorption is rate-limiting, and that the data may point towards stronger H(D) adsorption? 7. Has TPO been performed on the as-synthesized 0.5Ti-Ni(Sn)/SiO2 catalysts? The SI notes that hydrolysis of the titanium precursor was allowed to occur in atmosphere and then calcination was performed at 300˚C for 1 hr. Do the authors have evidence that the TiOx-phase formed, which remains amorphous, does not still contain carbonaceous species? 8. The paper assumes that Sn is reduced in-situ (in the discussion and DFT calculations). But it seems likely that Sn may partially oxidize when interaction with TiOx overlayers. Could this be addressed? 9. Further, it seems that Sn incorporation into Ni may change the structure or nature of the TiOx overlayer or alloy surface structure) (e.g. TiOx causes Ni domain aggregation and Sn aggregation). Can the authors comment on this?

Reviewer 1 Comment 1-1: The noteworthy results are the improved on stream performance due to reduced coking. This is a very active area of research and there are lots of groups trying to develop materials for efficient direct deoxygenation of biofuel-related materials to improve the heating value of the materials. As an example, Fuel (334) 2023 "Enhanced deoxygenation performance and coke resistance of Ni-based catalysts for jatropha oil conversion by rare earth elements" is one such example. It is often difficult to compare one catalytic paper to another because there are so many variables, but while this paper represents a nice result, it is difficult to describe it as particularly novel or particularly significant. Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s recognition of the noteworthy results of our work. We agree with the reviewer that the extensive research variables in the field of HDO make comparative evaluation of catalytic performance rather challenging. For instance, the article mentioned by the reviewer reports that modification of Ni catalyst by Er element improves both activity and coke resistance in jatropha oil deoxygenation at 340 °C under 3 MPa H . The application background, reactant and 2 reaction pressure differ significantly from those in our work, thereby limiting direct comparability between the studies. Since our work focuses on the HDO of m-cresol, a lignin-derived phenolic compound in bio-oils from fast pyrolysis that conducted under atmospheric pressure (Fig. 1a below), we review reports of phenolic HDO reactions in atmospheric fixed-bed reactor and evaluate the stability of different catalysts. There are still hundreds of strongly related studies, indicating that this remains a very active area, as the reviewer pointed out. From the survey, we found that most studies have focused on designing bifunctional catalysts to enhance the activity and selectivity in phenolic HDO reactions, whereas relatively fewer have addressed catalyst stability. The above Table R1 shows that most catalysts undergo rapid deactivation in 5 h, with the percentage decrease of conversion ranging from 15% to 89.9%. Fig. 1 Interfacial catalysis strategies for phenolic HDO reactions under atmospheric pressure. a Schematic of HDO units integrated into biomass fast pyrolysis process for biofuel production. b Summary of previous studies on improving metal catalyst performance via interfacial site construction. c Design of the inverse TiO -NiSn alloy interface with efficient HDO performance and anti-coking stability. x A few groups have proposed excellent strategies to improve catalyst stability (Fig. 1b). For instance, Yang et al. reported that a small amount of nitrogen doping in the carbon support reduces the deactivation rate of Fe particles almost by one order of magnitude in m-cresol HDO (ACS Catal. 2020, 10, 7884−7893), and Teles et al. found that Ce-enriched catalysts exhibit higher HDO stability because of the reduced oxophilicity on catalyst (ACS Catal. 2017, 7, 2058−2073). However, in these cases, the enhanced catalyst stability comes with a substantial sacrifice in activity. Thus, engineering phenolic HDO catalysts with both high efficiency and anti-coking stability at atmospheric pressure remains a significant challenge. Our work proposes the inverse TiO -NiSn alloy interface to solve the above problem. x The Ni metal induced coking is suppressed by the formation of NiSn alloy, while the enhanced activity is achieved by the formation of highly active TiO -NiSn alloy x interface. In addition, the inverse interface structure is applied instead of traditional interface structure using TiO support, thus suppressing the acid induced coking. Thus, 2 an effective, non-noble metal catalyst is obtained with high HDO selectivity, enhanced activity and anti-coking stability (Fig. 1c). By the above comparison and discussion, we believe that our strategy represents a meaningful advancement and novelty in the field. Action: Following the comment of the reviewer, we have added the above Fig. 1 to the introduction of manuscript to highlight the advantages of the inverse TiO -NiSn/SiO x 2 catalyst in this field, and the first three paragraphs of introduction have been rewritten: “Fast pyrolysis is an efficient technology on biomass conversion to sustainable liquid fuels, which can produce bio-oil with a yield up to 75 wt%1,2. But the bio-oil presents shortcomings such as high oxygen content and poor stability, requiring hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) treatment to improve its quality before application as fuel. HDO is also a key reaction in catalytic fast pyrolysis, and the development of effective HDO catalysts operable under ambient-pressure conditions could further improve overall process integration (Fig. 1a)3,4. Among common oxygen-containing structures in bio-oil, cleavage of the phenolic C-O bond is the most challenging5. Thus, the development of high-performance phenolic HDO catalysts has attracted widespread attention. Despite this, most reported HDO reactions operate in batch systems or require high H pressure, while vapor-phase HDO studies under atmospheric pressure that 2 compatible with pyrolysis conditions are still limited6. Effective HDO catalysis typically requires not only C-O bond activation but also hydrogenation and dehydrogenation steps. To minimize H overconsumption, 2 suppressing aromatic ring hydrogenation is essential. Additionally, the catalyst must inhibit both C-C bond cleavage and coking side reactions to ensure target product selectivity and maintain long-term stability. These requirements are difficult to achieve with mono transition metal catalysts, whereas interfacial structures offer a promising solution due to their multifunctionality and flexible designability (Fig. 1b)7. For instance, numerous studies have reported that constructing metal-acidic/oxophilic site interfaces can significantly enhance both activity and selectivity in phenolic HDO reactions. In such systems, the acid sites can be provided by amorphous SiO -Al O , 2 2 3 zeolites, or other acidic solids, while the oxophilic sites usually originate from transition metals or metal oxides with strong oxygen affinity8. On such interfaces, it has been revealed that the phenyl ring preferentially adsorbs on the metal site, while the hydroxyl group of phenols binds to neighboring acidic/oxophilic sites. This synergistic activation leads to a lower energy barrier for C-O cleavage and enhanced HDO activity, in contrast to less selective phenyl ring activation on metal sites alone or the inefficient oxygen activation on acidic/oxophilic sites alone9,10. However, the phenolic reactants tend to form condensed-ring compounds, leading to catalyst deactivation by coking11,12. The acidic/oxophilic sites facilitate the condensation process of phenolic intermediates and thereby accelerate coking13-15. For instance, several studies have reported faster deactivation on acidic/reducible oxide supported catalysts than those on inert SiO 2 supported catalysts16,17. Unlike the above strategies, some researchers have used non-acidic/non-oxophilic materials to construct interface active sites with metals, achieving progress in improving coke resistance (Fig. 1b). Yang et al. reported that a small amount of nitrogen doping in the carbon support reduces the deactivation rate of Fe particles almost by one order of magnitude in m-cresol HDO, which is attributed to the reduced oxygen affinity of Fe by N species18. Teles et al. investigated the influence of Ce/Zr ratio on phenol HDO performance over Pd/Ce Zr O catalysts. They found that Ce-enriched catalysts x 1-x 2 exhibit higher stability, which is attributed to the reduced oxophilicity19. However, in these cases, the enhanced catalyst stability comes with a substantial sacrifice in activity. Thus, engineering phenolic HDO catalysts with both high efficiency and anti-coking stability under atmospheric pressure remains a significant challenge.” The first three sentences in Abstract have been revised to: “Hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) of phenolics is crucial for lignin-to-fuel production via fast pyrolysis. The reaction under atmospheric H pressure offers compatibility with pyrolysis conditions, high 2 aromatic selectivity and low H consumption, but suffers from coking-induced catalyst 2 deactivation. In this work, we report a TiO -decorated NiSn/SiO catalyst (Ti- x 2 NiSn/SiO ), achieving 100% deoxygenation selectivity and enhanced stability in m- 2 cresol HDO. The superior performance stems from:”. Comment 1-2: The experimental result is a bit underdeveloped in parts. The uploaded file provides more detail on what aspects need to be expanded. It also notes grammatical errors. As written there is not enough detail in the experimental section for the work to be reproduced, but this could be addressed in a revision. The phrase here is intended to succinctly describe the trade-off we made, but we agree that a more detailed explanation is necessary. The primary reason for selecting a 2×2×1 k-point grid is the large size of our computational model. After considering the size of NiSn alloy, TiO cluster and m- x cresol molecule, we decide to construct a 6×6 periodic model comprising over 130 atoms. For systems of this scale, the computational cost for structural optimization and frequency calculations increases dramatically with k-point density. Our choice is guided by the following specific considerations: (1) System size and k-point sensitivity: Large supercells have a small Brillouin zone. Consequently, a relatively sparse k-point mesh is often sufficient to achieve convergence for relative energies (e.g., adsorption energies, reaction barriers), which are the key properties reported in our study. The absolute total energy is indeed sensitive to k-points, but the differences in total energy between similar configurations (which determine relative energies) converge much faster. (2) Convergence testing for relative energies: To ensure reliability, we compared the adsorption energy of m-cresol using a 2×2×1 grid versus a more computationally expensive 3×3×1 grid. The difference was found to be less than 0.05 eV, which is negligible for the comparative and mechanistic conclusions of our study. Increasing the grid beyond 2×2×1 would thus provide little improvement in accuracy for relative energies at a higher computational cost. Additionally, for ZPE corrections, we fixed all substrate atoms and only computed the vibrations of the adsorbate species. This is a standard practice to obtain accurate vibrational modes related to the surface reaction while conserving computational resources. ### Reviewer 1

The noteworthy results are the improved on stream performance due to reduced coking. This is a very active area of research and there are lots of groups trying to develop materials for efficient direct deoxygenation of biofuel-related materials to improve the heating value of the materials. As an example, Fuel (334) 2023 "Enhanced deoxygenation performance and coke resistance of Ni-based catalysts for jatropha oil conversion by rare earth elements" is one such example. It is often difficult to compare one catalytic paper to another because there are so many variables, but while this paper represents a nice result, it is difficult to describe it as particularly novel or particularly significant. The experimental result is a bit underdeveloped in parts. The uploaded file provides more detail on what aspects need to be expanded. It also notes grammatical errors. As written there is not enough detail in the experimental section for the work to be reproduced, but this could be addressed in a revision. More detail is also needed on number of replicates and error propagation needs to be clearly articulated and error bars included on all catalytic data. The structure of the manuscript undercuts its potential impact. The whole idea of spending 12 pages discussing the first generation catalyst only to then switch to a second generation catalyst does not seem like an efficient or effective way to present this information. The aper would be more impactful if it begins with what works best and perhaps the discussion of the first generation catalyst can be mentioned briefly and mostly moved to SI.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, the authors study TiO2-functionalized, bimetallic catalysts for hydrodeoxygenation of m-cresol, which is a much-studied reaction. This work essentially combines two ideas that have been in the literature for a while: adding Sn to Ni to reduce the tendency toward coke formation, and using TiO2 modifiers on the surface of the catalyst to improve interfacial activity. The authors discover some interesting synergistic effects. For example, whereas TiO2-supported Ni3Sn catalysts are active but not especially stable, producing inverse catalysts in which the TiO2 is located above the catalyst particles produces an active and stable catalyst. The authors largely do an excellent job of characterizing the prepared materials and analyzing the key reaction process with computational methods. Although some of the basic concepts that motivated the paper have been well-established, for me there is clearly sufficient novelty in the results to justify publication in Nature Comm. I recommend that the authors consider the following few points as they revise their manuscript. 1. Regarding Figure 1C, did the authors perform a control in which DRIFTS was done after adsorption of cresol on the support only? Sometimes it can be difficult to use DRIFTS to probe interfacial sites specifically, and some of these compounds may adsorb on support sites far from the interface. 2. The authors claim that the inverse strategy is beneficial because the TiOx on the surface has a lower acidity, allowing improved lifetime. However, I did not see where this proposal was tested experimentally. Can the authors elaborate on the evidence that supports their proposal? An alternative proposal is that TiO2 could block sites that ultimately lead to coking. I understand why the authors proposed that surface acidity is the driving factor, but the manuscript would be improved by describing the evidence for this proposal. 3. Since the TiO2 clusters appear from experimental data to bind to undercoordinated sites on the catalyst surface, did the DFT studies consider use of a stepped surface rather than a (111) surface for any exploratory calculations? Even if not, could the authors comment on whether the (111) surface would be expected to serve as a useful model? 4. Although the mechanistic proposal from the DFT calculations seems similar to that from Janik and coworkers (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcat.2019.07.012), the authors may want to comment more on the subsequent steps of the catalytic cycle, as in the prior work. It is not so surprising that a reduced Ti3O5 cluster will interact strongly with the O atom of m-cresol, especially on a Sn-doped surface where the interaction of the cluster with the surface is weaker. The key step on such a surface may be regeneration of the oxygen vacancy, which is only briefly discussed here in reference Figure S17. It wasn’t so clear to me: did the authors compute the activation barrier for oxygen vacancy creation? It appears that the energy required to create such a vacancy was similar for the Ni and Ni3Sn surfaces, which I find somewhat surprising given the other effects of Sn. In any case, I think the authors should talk more about the full cycle. Minor comments / typos: Line 138: “In contract” should be “In contrast” Line 192: “chemistry” should be “chemical” Line 205: the word “spectroscopy” should appear after “transform”, and the acronym should say “DRIFTS”. Line 448: “strength” should be “strong”

### Reviewer 3

This work reports on the study of TiOx-modified Ni(Sn) catalysts for the hydrodeoxygenation of m-cresol through reactivity measurements, characterization, and theoretical calculations. The work follows a consistent narrative which introduces logically increasing complexity, first through the formation of NiSn alloy nanoparticles to improve HDO reactivity and stability over Ni nanoparticles, followed by the decoration of NiSn alloy nanoparticles with TiOx to facilitate reactivity. The authors conclude that TiOx and NiSn phases interact synergistically to enable enhanced HDO by reduced C-O activation barriers and inhibited deactivation mechanisms. However, there are some questions that remain after reading the manuscript as is that should be addressed prior to consideration for publication. Those questions are: 1. Through the manuscript, the authors are inconsistent in their assignment of deactivation behaviors. At times, they cite work which relates the formation of oxide overlayers (SMSI) to the deactivation of Ni sites by physical coverage and prevention of adsorption. Other times, they discuss the formation of coke at acidic TiOx sites. In the end, there does not seem to be a conclusion reached on which is relevant, or whether both contribute in this experimental system and sometimes the authors could be more quantitative. 2. For example, in the comparison of Ni/TiO2 and Ni/SiO2, the TiO2 supported material deactivates from 95 to 5% conversion whereas Ni/SiO2 deactivates from 95% to 50% conversion. Is this consistent with the 2x amount of C deposition for Ni/TiO2 compared to Ni/SiO2? 3. Staying on the note about deactivation – the authors focus on the acidity of TiO2 as a mediator for coke formation and thus deactivation. Upon formation of interaction between Sn and TiOx, the authors observe increased stability – this would lead one to consider that Sn has reduced the acidity of TiOx. How would this happen? What chemical effect would lead to this? 4. The estimation of TiOx coverage by CO DRIFTS is potentially not reliable, which the authors attempt to convey by calling the results “semi-quantitative”. Can the authors provide further detail about their DRIFTS quantification so that an assessment of the validity of their approach can be made? Is the quantification different if absorbance units are used instead of Kubelka-Munk? Is it possible to conduct a more quantitative analysis such as CO pulsed chemisorption? 5. Do the authors have insight into the experimental error for their temperature-dependent reaction measurements made to assess apparent activation barriers? What is the statistical significance of the difference in barriers between these two materials? 6. I have questions about the H/D exchange experiments and their analysis. The authors approach the data with the assumption that H2(D2) activation is rate-limiting in the case of all catalysts. Could it not also be that HD desorption is rate-limiting, and that the data may point towards stronger H(D) adsorption? 7. Has TPO been performed on the as-synthesized 0.5Ti-Ni(Sn)/SiO2 catalysts? The SI notes that hydrolysis of the titanium precursor was allowed to occur in atmosphere and then calcination was performed at 300˚C for 1 hr. Do the authors have evidence that the TiOx-phase formed, which remains amorphous, does not still contain carbonaceous species? 8. The paper assumes that Sn is reduced in-situ (in the discussion and DFT calculations). But it seems likely that Sn may partially oxidize when interaction with TiOx overlayers. Could this be addressed? 9. Further, it seems that Sn incorporation into Ni may change the structure or nature of the TiOx overlayer or alloy surface structure) (e.g. TiOx causes Ni domain aggregation and Sn aggregation). Can the authors comment on this?

### Reviewer 4

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The noteworthy results are the improved on stream performance due to reduced coking. This is a very active area of research and there are lots of groups trying to develop materials for efficient direct deoxygenation of biofuel-related materials to improve the heating value of the materials. As an example, Fuel (334) 2023 "Enhanced deoxygenation performance and coke resistance of Ni-based catalysts for jatropha oil conversion by rare earth elements" is one such example. It is often difficult to compare one catalytic paper to another because there are so many variables, but while this paper represents a nice result, it is difficult to describe it as particularly novel or particularly significant. The experimental result is a bit underdeveloped in parts. The uploaded file provides more detail on what aspects need to be expanded. It also notes grammatical errors. As written there is not enough detail in the experimental section for the work to be reproduced, but this could be addressed in a revision. More detail is also needed on number of replicates and error propagation needs to be clearly articulated and error bars included on all catalytic data. The structure of the manuscript undercuts its potential impact. The whole idea of spending 12 pages discussing the first generation catalyst only to then switch to a second generation catalyst does not seem like an efficient or effective way to present this information. The aper would be more impactful if it begins with what works best and perhaps the discussion of the first generation catalyst can be mentioned briefly and mostly moved to SI.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, the authors study TiO2-functionalized, bimetallic catalysts for hydrodeoxygenation of m-cresol, which is a much-studied reaction. This work essentially combines two ideas that have been in the literature for a while: adding Sn to Ni to reduce the tendency toward coke formation, and using TiO2 modifiers on the surface of the catalyst to improve interfacial activity. The authors discover some interesting synergistic effects. For example, whereas TiO2-supported Ni3Sn catalysts are active but not especially stable, producing inverse catalysts in which the TiO2 is located above the catalyst particles produces an active and stable catalyst. The authors largely do an excellent job of characterizing the prepared materials and analyzing the key reaction process with computational methods. Although some of the basic concepts that motivated the paper have been well-established, for me there is clearly sufficient novelty in the results to justify publication in Nature Comm. I recommend that the authors consider the following few points as they revise their manuscript. 1. Regarding Figure 1C, did the authors perform a control in which DRIFTS was done after adsorption of cresol on the support only? Sometimes it can be difficult to use DRIFTS to probe interfacial sites specifically, and some of these compounds may adsorb on support sites far from the interface. 2. The authors claim that the inverse strategy is beneficial because the TiOx on the surface has a lower acidity, allowing improved lifetime. However, I did not see where this proposal was tested experimentally. Can the authors elaborate on the evidence that supports their proposal? An alternative proposal is that TiO2 could block sites that ultimately lead to coking. I understand why the authors proposed that surface acidity is the driving factor, but the manuscript would be improved by describing the evidence for this proposal. 3. Since the TiO2 clusters appear from experimental data to bind to undercoordinated sites on the catalyst surface, did the DFT studies consider use of a stepped surface rather than a (111) surface for any exploratory calculations? Even if not, could the authors comment on whether the (111) surface would be expected to serve as a useful model? 4. Although the mechanistic proposal from the DFT calculations seems similar to that from Janik and coworkers (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcat.2019.07.012), the authors may want to comment more on the subsequent steps of the catalytic cycle, as in the prior work. It is not so surprising that a reduced Ti3O5 cluster will interact strongly with the O atom of m-cresol, especially on a Sn-doped surface where the interaction of the cluster with the surface is weaker. The key step on such a surface may be regeneration of the oxygen vacancy, which is only briefly discussed here in reference Figure S17. It wasn’t so clear to me: did the authors compute the activation barrier for oxygen vacancy creation? It appears that the energy required to create such a vacancy was similar for the Ni and Ni3Sn surfaces, which I find somewhat surprising given the other effects of Sn. In any case, I think the authors should talk more about the full cycle. Minor comments / typos: Line 138: “In contract” should be “In contrast” Line 192: “chemistry” should be “chemical” Line 205: the word “spectroscopy” should appear after “transform”, and the acronym should say “DRIFTS”. Line 448: “strength” should be “strong”

### Reviewer 3

This work reports on the study of TiOx-modified Ni(Sn) catalysts for the hydrodeoxygenation of m-cresol through reactivity measurements, characterization, and theoretical calculations. The work follows a consistent narrative which introduces logically increasing complexity, first through the formation of NiSn alloy nanoparticles to improve HDO reactivity and stability over Ni nanoparticles, followed by the decoration of NiSn alloy nanoparticles with TiOx to facilitate reactivity. The authors conclude that TiOx and NiSn phases interact synergistically to enable enhanced HDO by reduced C-O activation barriers and inhibited deactivation mechanisms. However, there are some questions that remain after reading the manuscript as is that should be addressed prior to consideration for publication. Those questions are: 1. Through the manuscript, the authors are inconsistent in their assignment of deactivation behaviors. At times, they cite work which relates the formation of oxide overlayers (SMSI) to the deactivation of Ni sites by physical coverage and prevention of adsorption. Other times, they discuss the formation of coke at acidic TiOx sites. In the end, there does not seem to be a conclusion reached on which is relevant, or whether both contribute in this experimental system and sometimes the authors could be more quantitative. 2. For example, in the comparison of Ni/TiO2 and Ni/SiO2, the TiO2 supported material deactivates from 95 to 5% conversion whereas Ni/SiO2 deactivates from 95% to 50% conversion. Is this consistent with the 2x amount of C deposition for Ni/TiO2 compared to Ni/SiO2? 3. Staying on the note about deactivation – the authors focus on the acidity of TiO2 as a mediator for coke formation and thus deactivation. Upon formation of interaction between Sn and TiOx, the authors observe increased stability – this would lead one to consider that Sn has reduced the acidity of TiOx. How would this happen? What chemical effect would lead to this? 4. The estimation of TiOx coverage by CO DRIFTS is potentially not reliable, which the authors attempt to convey by calling the results “semi-quantitative”. Can the authors provide further detail about their DRIFTS quantification so that an assessment of the validity of their approach can be made? Is the quantification different if absorbance units are used instead of Kubelka-Munk? Is it possible to conduct a more quantitative analysis such as CO pulsed chemisorption? 5. Do the authors have insight into the experimental error for their temperature-dependent reaction measurements made to assess apparent activation barriers? What is the statistical significance of the difference in barriers between these two materials? 6. I have questions about the H/D exchange experiments and their analysis. The authors approach the data with the assumption that H2(D2) activation is rate-limiting in the case of all catalysts. Could it not also be that HD desorption is rate-limiting, and that the data may point towards stronger H(D) adsorption? 7. Has TPO been performed on the as-synthesized 0.5Ti-Ni(Sn)/SiO2 catalysts? The SI notes that hydrolysis of the titanium precursor was allowed to occur in atmosphere and then calcination was performed at 300˚C for 1 hr. Do the authors have evidence that the TiOx-phase formed, which remains amorphous, does not still contain carbonaceous species? 8. The paper assumes that Sn is reduced in-situ (in the discussion and DFT calculations). But it seems likely that Sn may partially oxidize when interaction with TiOx overlayers. Could this be addressed? 9. Further, it seems that Sn incorporation into Ni may change the structure or nature of the TiOx overlayer or alloy surface structure) (e.g. TiOx causes Ni domain aggregation and Sn aggregation). Can the authors comment on this?

After considering the size of NiSn alloy, TiO cluster and m- x cresol molecule, we decide to construct a 6×6 periodic model comprising over 130 atoms. For systems of this scale, the computational cost for structural optimization and frequency calculations increases dramatically with k-point density. Our choice is guided by the following specific considerations: (1) System size and k-point sensitivity: Large supercells have a small Brillouin zone. The difference was found to be less than 0.05 eV, which is negligible for the comparative and mechanistic conclusions of our study. Increasing the grid beyond 2×2×1 would thus provide little improvement in accuracy for relative energies at a higher computational cost. Additionally, for ZPE corrections, we fixed all substrate atoms and only computed the vibrations of the adsorbate species. ## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The noteworthy results are the improved on stream performance due to reduced coking. This is a very active area of research and there are lots of groups trying to develop materials for efficient direct deoxygenation of biofuel-related materials to improve the heating value of the materials. As an example, Fuel (334) 2023 "Enhanced deoxygenation performance and coke resistance of Ni-based catalysts for jatropha oil conversion by rare earth elements" is one such example. It is often difficult to compare one catalytic paper to another because there are so many variables, but while this paper represents a nice result, it is difficult to describe it as particularly novel or particularly significant. The experimental result is a bit underdeveloped in parts. The uploaded file provides more detail on what aspects need to be expanded. It also notes grammatical errors. As written there is not enough detail in the experimental section for the work to be reproduced, but this could be addressed in a revision. More detail is also needed on number of replicates and error propagation needs to be clearly articulated and error bars included on all catalytic data. The structure of the manuscript undercuts its potential impact. The whole idea of spending 12 pages discussing the first generation catalyst only to then switch to a second generation catalyst does not seem like an efficient or effective way to present this information. The aper would be more impactful if it begins with what works best and perhaps the discussion of the first generation catalyst can be mentioned briefly and mostly moved to SI.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, the authors study TiO2-functionalized, bimetallic catalysts for hydrodeoxygenation of m-cresol, which is a much-studied reaction. This work essentially combines two ideas that have been in the literature for a while: adding Sn to Ni to reduce the tendency toward coke formation, and using TiO2 modifiers on the surface of the catalyst to improve interfacial activity. The authors discover some interesting synergistic effects. For example, whereas TiO2-supported Ni3Sn catalysts are active but not especially stable, producing inverse catalysts in which the TiO2 is located above the catalyst particles produces an active and stable catalyst. The authors largely do an excellent job of characterizing the prepared materials and analyzing the key reaction process with computational methods. Although some of the basic concepts that motivated the paper have been well-established, for me there is clearly sufficient novelty in the results to justify publication in Nature Comm. I recommend that the authors consider the following few points as they revise their manuscript. 1. Regarding Figure 1C, did the authors perform a control in which DRIFTS was done after adsorption of cresol on the support only? Sometimes it can be difficult to use DRIFTS to probe interfacial sites specifically, and some of these compounds may adsorb on support sites far from the interface. 2. The authors claim that the inverse strategy is beneficial because the TiOx on the surface has a lower acidity, allowing improved lifetime. However, I did not see where this proposal was tested experimentally. Can the authors elaborate on the evidence that supports their proposal? An alternative proposal is that TiO2 could block sites that ultimately lead to coking. I understand why the authors proposed that surface acidity is the driving factor, but the manuscript would be improved by describing the evidence for this proposal. 3. Since the TiO2 clusters appear from experimental data to bind to undercoordinated sites on the catalyst surface, did the DFT studies consider use of a stepped surface rather than a (111) surface for any exploratory calculations? Even if not, could the authors comment on whether the (111) surface would be expected to serve as a useful model? 4. Although the mechanistic proposal from the DFT calculations seems similar to that from Janik and coworkers (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcat.2019.07.012), the authors may want to comment more on the subsequent steps of the catalytic cycle, as in the prior work. It is not so surprising that a reduced Ti3O5 cluster will interact strongly with the O atom of m-cresol, especially on a Sn-doped surface where the interaction of the cluster with the surface is weaker. The key step on such a surface may be regeneration of the oxygen vacancy, which is only briefly discussed here in reference Figure S17. It wasn’t so clear to me: did the authors compute the activation barrier for oxygen vacancy creation? It appears that the energy required to create such a vacancy was similar for the Ni and Ni3Sn surfaces, which I find somewhat surprising given the other effects of Sn. In any case, I think the authors should talk more about the full cycle. Minor comments / typos: Line 138: “In contract” should be “In contrast” Line 192: “chemistry” should be “chemical” Line 205: the word “spectroscopy” should appear after “transform”, and the acronym should say “DRIFTS”. Line 448: “strength” should be “strong”

### Reviewer 3

This work reports on the study of TiOx-modified Ni(Sn) catalysts for the hydrodeoxygenation of m-cresol through reactivity measurements, characterization, and theoretical calculations. The work follows a consistent narrative which introduces logically increasing complexity, first through the formation of NiSn alloy nanoparticles to improve HDO reactivity and stability over Ni nanoparticles, followed by the decoration of NiSn alloy nanoparticles with TiOx to facilitate reactivity. The authors conclude that TiOx and NiSn phases interact synergistically to enable enhanced HDO by reduced C-O activation barriers and inhibited deactivation mechanisms. However, there are some questions that remain after reading the manuscript as is that should be addressed prior to consideration for publication. Those questions are: 1. Through the manuscript, the authors are inconsistent in their assignment of deactivation behaviors. At times, they cite work which relates the formation of oxide overlayers (SMSI) to the deactivation of Ni sites by physical coverage and prevention of adsorption. Other times, they discuss the formation of coke at acidic TiOx sites. In the end, there does not seem to be a conclusion reached on which is relevant, or whether both contribute in this experimental system and sometimes the authors could be more quantitative. 2. For example, in the comparison of Ni/TiO2 and Ni/SiO2, the TiO2 supported material deactivates from 95 to 5% conversion whereas Ni/SiO2 deactivates from 95% to 50% conversion. Is this consistent with the 2x amount of C deposition for Ni/TiO2 compared to Ni/SiO2? 3. Staying on the note about deactivation – the authors focus on the acidity of TiO2 as a mediator for coke formation and thus deactivation. Upon formation of interaction between Sn and TiOx, the authors observe increased stability – this would lead one to consider that Sn has reduced the acidity of TiOx. How would this happen? What chemical effect would lead to this? 4. The estimation of TiOx coverage by CO DRIFTS is potentially not reliable, which the authors attempt to convey by calling the results “semi-quantitative”. Can the authors provide further detail about their DRIFTS quantification so that an assessment of the validity of their approach can be made? Is the quantification different if absorbance units are used instead of Kubelka-Munk? Is it possible to conduct a more quantitative analysis such as CO pulsed chemisorption? 5. Do the authors have insight into the experimental error for their temperature-dependent reaction measurements made to assess apparent activation barriers? What is the statistical significance of the difference in barriers between these two materials? 6. I have questions about the H/D exchange experiments and their analysis. The authors approach the data with the assumption that H2(D2) activation is rate-limiting in the case of all catalysts. Could it not also be that HD desorption is rate-limiting, and that the data may point towards stronger H(D) adsorption? 7. Has TPO been performed on the as-synthesized 0.5Ti-Ni(Sn)/SiO2 catalysts? The SI notes that hydrolysis of the titanium precursor was allowed to occur in atmosphere and then calcination was performed at 300˚C for 1 hr. Do the authors have evidence that the TiOx-phase formed, which remains amorphous, does not still contain carbonaceous species? 8. The paper assumes that Sn is reduced in-situ (in the discussion and DFT calculations). But it seems likely that Sn may partially oxidize when interaction with TiOx overlayers. Could this be addressed? 9. Further, it seems that Sn incorporation into Ni may change the structure or nature of the TiOx overlayer or alloy surface structure) (e.g. TiOx causes Ni domain aggregation and Sn aggregation). Can the authors comment on this?

Our work proposes the inverse TiO -NiSn alloy interface to solve the above problem. x The Ni metal induced coking is suppressed by the formation of NiSn alloy, while the enhanced activity is achieved by the formation of highly active TiO -NiSn alloy x interface. In addition, the inverse interface structure is applied instead of traditional interface structure using TiO support, thus suppressing the acid induced coking. Thus, 2 an effective, non-noble metal catalyst is obtained with high HDO selectivity, enhanced activity and anti-coking stability (Fig. 1c). Action: Following the comment of the reviewer, we have added the above Fig. 1 to the introduction of manuscript to highlight the advantages of the inverse TiO -NiSn/SiO x 2 catalyst in this field, and the first three paragraphs of introduction have been rewritten: “Fast pyrolysis is an efficient technology on biomass conversion to sustainable liquid fuels, which can produce bio-oil with a yield up to 75 wt%1,2. But the bio-oil presents shortcomings such as high oxygen content and poor stability, requiring hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) treatment to improve its quality before application as fuel. HDO is also a key reaction in catalytic fast pyrolysis, and the development of effective HDO catalysts operable under ambient-pressure conditions could further improve overall process integration (Fig. 1a)3,4. Among common oxygen-containing structures in bio-oil, cleavage of the phenolic C-O bond is the most challenging5. Thus, the development of high-performance phenolic HDO catalysts has attracted widespread attention. Despite this, most reported HDO reactions operate in batch systems or require high H pressure, while vapor-phase HDO studies under atmospheric pressure that 2 compatible with pyrolysis conditions are still limited6. Effective HDO catalysis typically requires not only C-O bond activation but also hydrogenation and dehydrogenation steps. To minimize H overconsumption, 2 suppressing aromatic ring hydrogenation is essential. Additionally, the catalyst must inhibit both C-C bond cleavage and coking side reactions to ensure target product selectivity and maintain long-term stability. These requirements are difficult to achieve with mono transition metal catalysts, whereas interfacial structures offer a promising solution due to their multifunctionality and flexible designability (Fig. 1b)7. For instance, numerous studies have reported that constructing metal-acidic/oxophilic site interfaces can significantly enhance both activity and selectivity in phenolic HDO reactions. In such systems, the acid sites can be provided by amorphous SiO -Al O , 2 2 3 zeolites, or other acidic solids, while the oxophilic sites usually originate from transition metals or metal oxides with strong oxygen affinity8. On such interfaces, it has been revealed that the phenyl ring preferentially adsorbs on the metal site, while the hydroxyl group of phenols binds to neighboring acidic/oxophilic sites. This synergistic activation leads to a lower energy barrier for C-O cleavage and enhanced HDO activity, in contrast to less selective phenyl ring activation on metal sites alone or the inefficient oxygen activation on acidic/oxophilic sites alone9,10. However, the phenolic reactants tend to form condensed-ring compounds, leading to catalyst deactivation by coking11,12. The acidic/oxophilic sites facilitate the condensation process of phenolic intermediates and thereby accelerate coking13-15. For instance, several studies have reported faster deactivation on acidic/reducible oxide supported catalysts than those on inert SiO 2 supported catalysts16,17. Unlike the above strategies, some researchers have used non-acidic/non-oxophilic materials to construct interface active sites with metals, achieving progress in improving coke resistance (Fig. 1b). Yang et al. reported that a small amount of nitrogen doping in the carbon support reduces the deactivation rate of Fe particles almost by one order of magnitude in m-cresol HDO, which is attributed to the reduced oxygen affinity of Fe by N species18. Teles et al. investigated the influence of Ce/Zr ratio on phenol HDO performance over Pd/Ce Zr O catalysts. They found that Ce-enriched catalysts x 1-x 2 exhibit higher stability, which is attributed to the reduced oxophilicity19. The primary reason for selecting a 2×2×1 k-point grid is the large size of our computational model. After considering the size of NiSn alloy, TiO cluster and m- x cresol molecule, we decide to construct a 6×6 periodic model comprising over 130 atoms. For systems of this scale, the computational cost for structural optimization and frequency calculations increases dramatically with k-point density. Our choice is guided by the following specific considerations: (1) System size and k-point sensitivity: Large supercells have a small Brillouin zone. Consequently, a relatively sparse k-point mesh is often sufficient to achieve convergence for relative energies (e.g., adsorption energies, reaction barriers), which are the key properties reported in our study. The absolute total energy is indeed sensitive to k-points, but the differences in total energy between similar configurations (which determine relative energies) converge much faster. (2) Convergence testing for relative energies: To ensure reliability, we compared the adsorption energy of m-cresol using a 2×2×1 grid versus a more computationally expensive 3×3×1 grid. The difference was found to be less than 0.05 eV, which is negligible for the comparative and mechanistic conclusions of our study. Increasing the grid beyond 2×2×1 would thus provide little improvement in accuracy for relative energies at a higher computational cost. Additionally, for ZPE corrections, we fixed all substrate atoms and only computed the vibrations of the adsorbate species. This is a standard practice to obtain accurate vibrational modes related to the surface reaction while conserving computational resources.
